$comment: The six course units. Source: UNITS in site/index.html (Nov 23, 2026 build). Weeks are course weeks, not calendar weeks.

units.title: Talk to Me: The Communication Process
units.blurb: Get comfortable in front of the room, learn how communication works, and set the ground rules for honest, original work.
plan: The communication process
The sender–receiver model and its key vocabulary, why nerves are normal, and low-stakes speaking practice.
Ethics and the self-introduction speech
Plagiarism, citing aloud, and the course AI policy. Speeches at the end of the week.

hs.name: Self-Introduction Speech
req: Bring one object that represents you and show it during the speech.
Share three things: where you are from, something you love doing, and a goal.
Open with a hook and close with a memorable last line.
One note card with key words only.

col.name: Personal Artifact Speech
req: Build the speech around one artifact that reveals something important about you.
Use a clear structure: introduction with thesis, three main points, conclusion.
Turn in a key-word speaking outline before you present.
Speak extemporaneously: rehearsed, not memorized or read.

units.title: Audience, Research & Structure
units.blurb: Learn the toolkit every later speech uses: know your audience, find credible sources in Gale, and organize ideas into an outline.
plan: Audience analysis and listening
Who is in the room and what they already know. Brainstorm a person for your Heritage Month speech.
Research with Gale
Credible versus weak sources, peer-reviewed filters, oral citations, and APA 7.
Organizing and outlining
Thesis statements, main points, organizational patterns, and using evidence.

hs.name: Research & Outline Lab
req: Choose your Heritage Month person (Unit 3).
Find 3 credible sources; at least 1 must come from Gale.
Write each source in APA format.
Fill in the outline template: introduction, three main points, conclusion.

col.name: Annotated Bibliography & Preparation Outline
req: Find 5 credible sources about your Heritage Month person; at least 2 peer-reviewed from Gale.
Write a 3–4 sentence annotation for each: what it says and how you will use it.
Format everything in APA 7.
Write a full-sentence preparation outline with a thesis, main points, and transitions.

units.title: Informative Speech: Heritage Month
units.blurb: Choose one person who is important to Hispanic heritage or Black history and teach the class about their life and impact. First semester speeches happen during Hispanic Heritage Month; second semester speeches happen during Black History Month.

fall.label: 1st semester · Hispanic Heritage Month
fall.when: Speeches happen during Hispanic Heritage Month (September 15–October 15).
fall.name: Hispanic Heritage Month Speech
fall.person: a person important to Hispanic heritage

spring.label: 2nd semester · Black History Month
spring.when: Speeches happen during Black History Month (February).
spring.name: Black History Month Speech
spring.person: a person important to Black history

plan: Informative speaking and strong openings
Introductions, conclusions, and transitions. Sign up for your person (no repeats in a class).
Presentation aids and rehearsal
Build slides with key words and strong visuals. Peer rehearsal with a timer.
Speeches
1st semester: during Hispanic Heritage Month. 2nd semester: during Black History Month.

hs.name: Heritage Month Speech
req: Choose {person}.
Three main points in order: early life and roots, achievements, challenges they overcame.
3 credible sources (at least 1 from Gale), cited out loud and on a References slide in APA.
Slides with at least 3 visuals that teach something.
Finish the body with a Legacy slide: why this still matters today.
Complete the Academic Integrity disclosure.

col.name: Heritage Month Speech
req: Choose {person}.
Organize chronologically: early life, achievements, challenges overcome, then legacy.
Connect their legacy to today, in Kansas City or nationally.
5 credible sources (2 peer-reviewed from Gale), cited aloud with credentials and listed in APA 7.
Turn in your preparation outline and a key-word speaking outline.
Complete the Academic Integrity disclosure.

units.title: How-To / Demonstration Speech
units.blurb: Teach the class to do something, step by step, with real props. Clear language and smooth delivery matter most here.
plan: Process speeches, language, and delivery
Chronological order, clear and concrete words, extemporaneous delivery. Gather props.
Rehearse and present
Full run-through with props and a timer, then speeches.

hs.name: How-To Speech
req: Demonstrate a process live with real props (no dangerous items, flames, or food that needs cooking in class).
4–6 clear steps in order, so the audience could repeat it.
Tell us why the skill is useful in your introduction.
1 credible source cited out loud.

col.name: Demonstration Speech
req: Demonstrate a process live with real props, and explain why each step matters.
Organize with a clear pattern (chronological or spatial) and signposts.
2 credible sources cited aloud with credentials.
Turn in a preparation outline. Practice until props are handled smoothly.

units.title: Narrative Speech: Tell Your Story
units.blurb: Tell a true story from your life that pulls the audience in and connects them to you.
plan: Stories that connect
Why stories work, the story arc, and choosing a story you are comfortable sharing. Plan it in the Story Builder.
Narrative speeches
Tell your story, cheer for your classmates, and reflect on what you learned.

hs.name: Narrative Speech: My True Story
req: Tell a true story from your own life. Pick a prompt from the Story Builder or use your own idea.
You choose what to share. A funny or everyday story counts just as much as a hard one.
Follow the story arc: hook, setting, build-up, turning point, what happened after, and the lesson.
Use vivid details: what you saw, heard, and felt. Show us; don’t just tell us.
End with what you learned and a closing line we will remember.
Speak from a note card of key words, not a script. No formal outline is needed: the Story Builder gives you the structure.

col.name: Narrative Speech: A Personal Story with Purpose
req: Tell a true personal story that builds to one clear theme or insight.
You choose what to share. A funny or everyday story counts just as much as a hard one.
Shape it with a full arc and a clear turning point; cut details that don’t serve the theme.
Use vivid, sensory language and at least two devices (dialogue, repetition, callback, metaphor).
Connect your story to the audience: why should it matter to them?
Speak extemporaneously from a key-word card. Plan with the Story Builder; no full outline is required.

units.title: Persuasive Speech
units.blurb: High school students argue one side of a ProCon question. College students give a community action speech that asks a real decision-maker to fix a local problem.
plan: Ethos, pathos, logos
High school: choose a ProCon question. College: learn Monroe’s Motivated Sequence and choose a community problem.
Reasoning, fallacies, and research
Spot weak arguments. Research in Gale; college students add a local source or interview.
Build and rehearse
Fill in the slide template, write your counterargument or objection, rehearse with a timer.
Speeches and celebration
Present, give peer feedback, and celebrate how much your speaking has grown.

hs.name: ProCon Persuasive Speech
req: Answer a question from Britannica ProCon and take a clear side.
Three arguments, each with a claim, cited evidence, explanation, and why it matters.
Use logos, ethos, and pathos; answer the strongest counterargument.
3 credible sources in APA; ProCon ideas in your own words.
Use the persuasive slide template and complete the Academic Integrity slide.

col.name: Community Action Speech
req: Choose a real problem in Kansas City, KCK, or our school and a decision-maker who can fix it.
Follow Monroe’s Motivated Sequence: attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action.
Answer the strongest objection to your plan with evidence.
5–7 sources: at least 2 peer-reviewed from Gale and 1 local. ProCon is background only.
End with a specific ask: who, what, and by when.
